supplied_texts.title: Source A: IA draft extract, section 4 "Exploring the model" (student's own draft)
supplied_texts.text:
Section 4: Exploring the model

I measured the temperature of a cup of tea every five minutes with a kitchen thermometer. The room temperature was 21 °C throughout.

Table 1. Temperature of the tea
t (minutes): 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30
T (°C): 85, 71, 60, 51, 45, 35.5

Newton's law of cooling, which Newton proved in the Principia in 1687, states that T(t) = T_room + A e^(−kt). Since the graph of T against t curves downwards, the data is clearly exponential. At t = 0, A = 85 − 21 = 64. To find k I used the points t = 0 and t = 10:
k = −ln(60/85) ÷ 10 = 0.0348 ≈ 0.035
So my model is T(t) = 21 + 64e^(−0.035t).

Testing the model: at t = 20 the model gives T = 52.8 °C, which is a percentage error of only 1.1% compared with the measured 45 °C, so the model is accurate. My calculator gave r² = 0.97, which proves that the data follows Newton's law of cooling. Using the model, the tea reaches a drinkable 40 °C when t = ln(19/64) ÷ (−0.035) = 34.7 minutes, so the half-life of the tea is 34.7 minutes.

Reflection: this exploration proves that Newton's law is correct, and the model can be used to predict the temperature of the tea at any time in the future.

strong_answer_must: Spot the main error in k: the student divided raw temperatures (60/85) instead of excess temperatures above the room (39/64). Recompute k = −ln(39/64)/10 = 0.0495 (≈ 0.05), not 0.0348, and show that the two-point value using t = 0 and t = 30, −ln(14.5/64)/30 = 0.0495, agrees.

Recommend and ideally show the linearisation test: ln(T − 21) at t = 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30 is 4.159, 3.912, 3.664, 3.401, 3.178, 2.674, which is close to linear; a least-squares line gives gradient ≈ −0.0494 (k ≈ 0.049), intercept ≈ 4.157 (A ≈ 63.9) and r² ≈ 0.9998. Linearity of ln(T − T_room) against t is the evidence for an exponential model, not 'the graph curves downwards'.

Check the t = 20 test honestly: with the student's k = 0.035 the prediction 21 + 64e^(−0.7) = 52.8 °C is arithmetically correct, but the percentage error against the measured 45 °C is (52.8 − 45)/45 ≈ 17%, not 1.1%. With k = 0.0495 the prediction is 44.8 °C (error ≈ 0.5%).
Show the wrong k fails at the end of the data: at t = 30 the student's model predicts 21 + 64e^(−1.05) ≈ 43.4 °C against 35.5 °C measured (about 22% error), while k ≈ 0.0495 predicts 35.5 °C.

Correct the 40 °C prediction: t = −ln(19/64)/k gives ≈ 24.5 min with k = 0.0495 (≈ 24.3 min with k = 0.05); note that 34.7 min is consistent with the student's own wrong k, so the slip is in k, not in this step.

Correct the half-life claim: a half-life here is the time for the excess temperature T − 21 to halve, equal to ln 2 / k ≈ 14 min (k = 0.0495) or ≈ 13.9 min (k = 0.05); 34.7 min is a time to reach 40 °C, not a half-life, and 'half-life of the tea' is not a meaningful phrase.

Correct the attribution: Newton's law of cooling was not 'proved in the Principia in 1687'; it is an empirical relationship published in an anonymous 1701 paper in the Philosophical Transactions that is generally attributed to Newton. Tag this as recalled knowledge and hedge accordingly; do not invent a page or title the specialist cannot verify.

Challenge 'r² = 0.97 proves Newton's law': r² measures the fit of a particular regression, not the truth of a physical law; ask which regression the calculator performed (on raw T, or on ln(T − 21)?) and note that a linearised fit on the correct model gives r² ≈ 0.9998, which is also not a 'proof'.

Challenge 'the model proves Newton's law is correct' and 'predicts the temperature at any time in the future': a model is validated within its data range (0 to 30 min), the exponential tends to 21 °C and can never go below room temperature, and the reflection should state assumptions (constant room temperature, uniform temperature in the cup, thermometer resolution, no evaporation or stirring) and limitations.

Give concrete additions for the mathematics: the linearised regression with residuals, a comparison table of measured vs predicted temperatures for both k values, the derivation of T = T_room + A e^(−kt) from dT/dt = −k(T − T_room) (separable differential equation; derivation may be above SL, so hedge or state it as context), and a sensitivity check of the 40 °C prediction to k.

Give a provisional, hedged judgement of the current standard rather than a definite score: state that IA criteria and mark bands should be verified against the current IB subject guide and the teacher, that the arithmetic error in k and the unjustified claims would currently cost marks for use of mathematics and reflection, and keep the word 'provisional' in every sentence that awards or estimates a mark.
Include a single Sources line in which the supplied draft is tagged 'supplied text' and any recalled history is tagged 'recalled, not consulted'.
pitfalls: Accepting k = 0.035 as correct, or 'correcting' it to another wrong value (e.g. ln(85/60)/10 = 0.0348, or using 39/64 but forgetting the minus sign).
Claiming the student's 52.8 °C is arithmetically wrong (it is right for k = 0.035; the wrong part is the 1.1% error claim), or recomputing the percentage error incorrectly.
Calling 34.7 minutes a half-life, or giving a half-life that is not ln 2 / k for the chosen k.
Fabricating IA criterion names, descriptors or exact mark bands as certain fact, or stating a definite score without the word 'provisional'.
Inventing a citation for Newton's law of cooling (e.g. a Principia proposition number, or a precise 1701 page or issue), or asserting the 1701 attribution as certain with no hedge.
Saying r² = 0.97 shows the model is valid, or the opposite error of dismissing r² as meaningless without explaining what it measures.
Altering the student's data values, or substituting the specialist's own invented data.
Missing the room-temperature subtraction error entirely and instead commenting only on presentation.
Leaving a logical leap in the answer itself, e.g. 'the linearised r² is 0.9998 so the law is proven'.
